Risk premium and rough volatility

Ofelia Bonesini Address: Department of Mathematics, London School of Economics and Political Science Email address: o.bonesini@lse.ac.uk , Antoine Jacquier Address: Department of Mathematics, Imperial College London Email address: a.jacquier@imperial.ac.uk and Aitor Muguruza Address: Department of Mathematics, Imperial College London and Kaiju Capital Management Email address: aitor.muguruza-gonzalez15@imperial.ac.uk
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

One the one hand, rough volatility has been shown to provide a consistent framework to capture the properties of stock price dynamics both under the historical measure and for pricing purposes. On the other hand, market price of volatility risk is a well-studied object in Financial Economics, and empirical estimates show it to be stochastic rather than deterministic. Starting from a rough volatility model under the historical measure, we take up this challenge and provide an analysis of the impact of such a non-deterministic risk for pricing purposes.

Key words and phrases: 
risk premium, fractional Brownian motion, rough volatility

Introduction

Rough volatility is a recent paradigm proposed by Gatheral, Jaisson and Rosenbaum [14], which has attracted the attention of many academics and practitioners thanks to its numerous attractive properties [7]. Despite some debate about whether volatility should be rough [1, 2, 16, 25], this class of models provides a general framework to analyse both time series of the instantaneous volatility (under the historical measure ℙ\mathbb{P}) and prices of financial derivatives (under the pricing measure ℚ\mathbb{Q}). Starting from a rough version of the Bergomi model [8] under ℙ\mathbb{P}, Bayer, Friz and Gatheral [6] showed that a deterministic market price of risk preserved its structure under ℚ\mathbb{Q} (somehow akin to the Heston model [17] specification).

However, the Financial Economics literature has long shown that this market price of risk, monitoring the transition from ℙ\mathbb{P} to ℚ\mathbb{Q} via Girsanov’s transform, is not constant nor deterministic but instead stochastic. Its estimation has been the source of long academic discussions, outside the scope of the present paper though, and we refer the interested reader to [4, 9, 10, 12, 20, 22] for some useful pointers. This of course has serious practical implications for risk management, and [15] are fascinating sources of information. We focus here on this particular bridge between ℙ\mathbb{P} and ℚ\mathbb{Q} and show, not surprisingly, that the required stochasticity of the market price of risk unfortunately breaks the structure of the rough Bergomi model under ℚ\mathbb{Q}. However, we link the Hölder regularity of the volatility process (lower in this class of rough models) with that of the change of measure, and design several specifications making the model tractable under ℚ\mathbb{Q}. While the rough Bergomi model tracks well the behaviour of the historical volatility, it is less powerful for option prices, especially when considering VIX smiles (which are more or less flat under this model). Our new setup allows for more flexibility there, while preserving the ℙ\mathbb{P}-tractability of the model.

Section 1 provides the technical setup and analysis of the market price of risk, while the design of useful continuous-time rough stochastic volatility models with non-deterministic market prices of risk is detailed in Section 2. Finally, in Section 3, we perform an empirical analysis, estimating risk premia from historical options data.

1. Rough volatility models and change of measure

Rough volatility models are a natural extension of classical stochastic volatility models. Starting from such a model under the historical measure ℙ\mathbb{P}, we characterise below its dynamics under martingale measures ℚ\mathbb{Q} equivalent to ℙ\mathbb{P}, which then, by the fundamental theorem of asset pricing, allows for arbitrage-free option pricing. Following [14] for example, we consider a rather general class of (rough) stochastic volatility models under ℙ\mathbb{P}, where the stock price process admits the following dynamics:

Proposition 1.2.

Under Assumption 1.1, 𝒟γ\mathcal{D}^{\gamma} is a locally integrable ℙ\mathbb{P}-local martingale on 𝕋\mathbb{T}.

Proof.

Since WℙW^{\mathbb{P}} and Wℙ,⟂W^{\mathbb{P},\perp} are independent Brownian motions (and so locally square-integrable local martingales), thus by [24, Section II, Theorem 20] the processes X1:=∫0⋅χu​d​WuℙX^{1}:=\int_{0}^{\cdot}\chi_{u}\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{P}}_{u} and X2:=∫0⋅γu​d​Wuℙ,⟂X^{2}:=\int_{0}^{\cdot}\gamma_{u}\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{P},\perp}_{u} are locally square-integrable local martingales. The sum of two locally square-integrable local martingales is so itself and hence so is X:=X1+X2X:=X^{1}+X^{2}. Finally, notice that the Radon-Nikodym derivative  𝒟γ\mathcal{D}^{\gamma} defined in (1.3) is precisely the stochastic exponential of XX and so a non-negative local martingale itself. This implies that 𝒟γ\mathcal{D}^{\gamma} is a positive super-martingale which together with the fact that 𝒟0γ=1\mathcal{D}^{\gamma}_{0}=1 yields 𝒟tγ∈L1\mathcal{D}^{\gamma}_{t}\in L^{1} for all t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T}. ∎

Remark 1.7.

Under Assumption 1.3, consider ρ≤0\rho\leq 0, some valid function ψ\psi and kernel kk, and the constant values γs=γ¯\gamma_{s}=\overline{\gamma} and μ¯=μs≤rs=r¯\overline{\mu}=\mu_{s}\leq r_{s}=\overline{r} for γ¯,μ¯,r¯∈ℝ\overline{\gamma},\overline{\mu},\overline{r}\in\mathbb{R} ensuring Assumption 1.3(iv), so that Theorem 1.6 applies. In this scenario, a sufficient condition for the change of measure to be well defined is that the physical drift must be smaller than the risk-free rate.

1.1. Rough volatility models via Generalised Fractional Operators

Many rough volatility models can be represented [18] in terms of Generalised Fractional Operators (GFOs), which are defined as follows [18, Definition 1.1]:

Definition 1.8.

For any β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), α∈(−β,1−β)\alpha\in(-\beta,1-\beta) and h∈𝒞b1​((0,∞))h\in\mathcal{C}^{1}_{b}((0,\infty)) such that h′​(⋅)≤0h^{\prime}(\cdot)\leq 0, the GFO associated to the kernel k⁡(x):=xα​h​(x)k(x):=x^{\alpha}h(x) applied to f∈Cβ​(ℝ)f\in C^{\beta}(\mathbb{R}) is defined as

(1.12) (𝒢α​f)​(t):={∫0t(f⁡(s)−f⁡(0))​dd​t​k​(t−s)​ds,if α∈[0,1−β),dd​t​∫0t(f⁡(s)−f⁡(0))​k​(t−s)​ds,if ​α∈(−β,0).(\mathcal{G}^{\alpha}f)(t):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}(f(s)-f(0))\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}k(t-s)\mathrm{d}s,&\text{if }\alpha\in[0,1-\beta),\\ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{0}^{t}(f(s)-f(0))k(t-s)\mathrm{d}s,&\text{if }\alpha\in(-\beta,0).\end{array}\right.

as well as the set Λβ,H:={λ∈𝒞β for some β∈(0,1] such that H−∈(−β,0) and λ⁡(0)=0}\displaystyle\Lambda_{\beta,H}:=\Big\{\lambda\in\mathcal{C}^{\beta}\text{ for some $\beta\in(0,1]$ such that $H_{-}\in(-\beta,0)$ and $\lambda(0)=0$}\Big\}. To this particular power-law kernel, the GFO (from Definition 1.8, since H−∈(−12,0)H_{-}\in(-\frac{1}{2},0)) reads

(𝒢H−​f)​(t)=dd​t​∫0t(f⁡(s)−f⁡(0))​𝚔H−​(t−s)​𝑑s.(\mathcal{G}^{H_{-}}f)(t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{0}^{t}(f(s)-f(0))\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(t-s)\mathrm{d}s.

Denote further

𝙺⁡(t,s):=∫0t𝚔H−​(u−s)​𝑑u=𝚔H+​(t−s)H+,\mathtt{K}(t,s):=\int_{0}^{t}\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(u-s)\mathrm{d}u=\frac{\mathtt{k}_{H_{+}}(t-s)}{H_{+}},

so that the corresponding GFO is precisely 1H+​𝒢H+\frac{1}{H_{+}}\mathcal{G}^{H_{+}}. To streamline notations and emphasise nice symmetries, we introduce the notations

From the properties of GFO [18, Proposition 1.2], then 𝔊+​λ∈𝒞β+H+\mathfrak{G}^{+}\lambda\in\mathcal{C}^{\beta+H_{+}} as soon as λ∈Λβ,H\lambda\in\Lambda_{\beta,H}.

Corollary 1.9 (GFO representation).

With the kernel 𝚔H−\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}} in (1.13) and λ∈Λβ,H\lambda\in\Lambda_{\beta,H}, the system (1.7) under the risk-neutral measure ℚ\mathbb{Q} can be rewritten as

{d​StSt=rt​d​t+vt​d​Wtℚ,vt=ψ⁡(t,(𝔊−​Zℚ)​(t)+(𝔊+​λ)​(t)).\left\{\begin{array}[]{rl}\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}S_{t}}{S_{t}}&=\displaystyle r_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{v_{t}}\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{Q}}_{t},\\ v_{t}&=\displaystyle\psi\Big(t,(\mathfrak{G}^{-}Z^{\mathbb{Q}})(t)+(\mathfrak{G}^{+}\lambda)(t)\Big).\end{array}\right.
Proof.

The fact that ∫0⋅𝚔H−(⋅−s)dZsℚ=𝔊−Zℚ\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\cdot}\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(\cdot-s)\mathrm{d}Z^{\mathbb{Q}}_{s}=\mathfrak{G}^{-}Z^{\mathbb{Q}} is straightforward by the properties of GFO in [18, Proposition 1.4]. Furthermore, for any λ∈Λβ,H\lambda\in\Lambda_{\beta,H} and any t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T},

∫0t𝚔H−​(t−s)​λs​𝑑s=∫0tdd​t​𝙺​(t,s)​(λs−λ0)​𝑑s=(𝔊+​λ)​(t).\int_{0}^{t}\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(t-s)\lambda_{s}\mathrm{d}s=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathtt{K}(t,s)(\lambda_{s}-\lambda_{0})\mathrm{d}s=\left(\mathfrak{G}^{+}\lambda\right)(t).

∎

Note that since 𝔊+​λ∈𝒞β+H+\mathfrak{G}^{+}\lambda\in\mathcal{C}^{\beta+H_{+}}, then the risk premium has sample paths with Hölder regularity greater than 12\frac{1}{2}, regardless of the value of HH.

2. Modelling the risk premium process: A practical approach

In practice, the process λ\lambda is directly modelled without resorting to a change of measure starting from γ\gamma. We now consider different modelling choices for the risk premium λ\lambda and analyse some of its properties. In spite of the formal derivation of Theorem 1.6, a numerical treatment of the integral ∫0t∙ds\int_{0}^{t}\bullet\;\mathrm{d}s is rather intricate. To overcome this issue, Bayer, Friz and Gatheral [6] elegantly came up with the forward variance form of rough volatility in the spirit of Bergomi [8]. We shall restrict ourselves to this functional form (defined below in (2.1)) for the remainder of the section. Consider (1.7) with ψ⁡(t,x)=ξ0​(t)​eν​x\psi(t,x)=\xi_{0}(t)\mathrm{e}^{\nu x}, with ξ0​(t):=𝔼⁡[vt|ℱ0]\xi_{0}(t):=\mathbb{E}[v_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{0}] and ν>0\nu>0. Then the risk-neutral dynamics in forward variance form read

(2.1) {d​StSt=rt​d​t+vt​d​Wtℚ,vt=ξ0​(t)​exp⁡(ν⁡(∫0t𝚔H−​(t−s)​d​Zsℚ+∫0t𝚔H−​(t−s)​λs​ds)).\left\{\begin{array}[]{rl}\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}S_{t}}{S_{t}}&=\displaystyle r_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{v_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{Q}}_{t},\\ v_{t}&=\displaystyle\xi_{0}(t)\exp\left(\nu\left(\int_{0}^{t}\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(t-s)\mathrm{d}Z^{\mathbb{Q}}_{s}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(t-s)\lambda_{s}\mathrm{d}s\right)\right).\end{array}\right.

In the remaining of this section, the process XℚX^{\mathbb{Q}} will denote a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-Brownian motion possibly correlated with WℚW^{\mathbb{Q}} and ZℚZ^{\mathbb{Q}}.

2.1. Risk premium driven by Itô diffusion

Generalised Fractional Operators provide a natural framework to model risk premium processes driven by diffusions. The statement below shows the details of such a construction. Recall that the Beta function is defined as 𝔅⁡(x,y):=∫01sx−1​(1−s)y−1​𝑑s\mathfrak{B}(x,y):=\int_{0}^{1}s^{x-1}(1-s)^{y-1}\mathrm{d}s, for x,y>0x,y>0.

Proposition 2.1.

(2.4) ×exp⁡{ν22​(𝚔2​H​(t−s)2​H+𝚔2​(H+1)​(t−s)2​H+2​(H+1)+ρ​𝚔2​H+​(t−s)H+2)},\displaystyle\times\exp\left\{\frac{\nu^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{\mathtt{k}_{2H}(t-s)}{2H}+\frac{\mathtt{k}_{2(H+1)}(t-s)}{2H_{+}^{2}(H+1)}+\rho\frac{\mathtt{k}_{2H_{+}}(t-s)}{H_{+}^{2}}\right)\right\},

where (𝒢H−​Zℚ)​(s,t):=∫0s𝚔H−​(t−u)​d​Zuℚ\left(\mathcal{G}^{H_{-}}Z^{\mathbb{Q}}\right)(s,t):=\int_{0}^{s}\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(t-u)\mathrm{d}Z^{\mathbb{Q}}_{u} for 0≤s≤t0\leq s\leq t, and similarly for (𝒢α+H+​Xℚ)​(s,t)\left(\mathcal{G}^{\alpha+H_{+}}X^{\mathbb{Q}}\right)(s,t).

We first prove (2.2), which follows from [18, Proposition 1.2] and the identities highlighted above in Corollary 1.9. Remark 2.2.

Since the instantaneous variance in this model is log-Normal, the results in [19, Proposition 3.1] and numerical methods therein still apply for the VIX with minimal changes.

2.2. A risk premium driven by a CIR process

A second natural choice is to consider the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) process

(2.5) d​Ysℚ=κ⁡(θ−Ysℚ)​d​s+σ​Ysℚ​d​Xsℚ,\displaystyle\mathrm{d}Y^{\mathbb{Q}}_{s}=\kappa(\theta-Y^{\mathbb{Q}}_{s})\mathrm{d}s+\sigma\sqrt{Y^{\mathbb{Q}}_{s}}\ \mathrm{d}X^{\mathbb{Q}}_{s},

with κ,θ,σ>0\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0. As tempting as this approach might seem, it is not trivial at all to compute the basic quantity 𝔼ℚ​[vt]\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[v_{t}] here, as the following proposition shows.

Proposition 2.3.

𝔼sℚ​[vt]=ξ0​(t)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s}^{\mathbb{Q}}[v_{t}]=\xi_{0}(t) exp⁡{ν⁡[(𝔊−​Zℚ)​(s,t)+(𝒢α+H+​Yℚ)​(s,t)]}\displaystyle\exp\Big\{\nu\left[\left(\mathfrak{G}^{-}Z^{\mathbb{Q}}\right)(s,t)+\left(\mathcal{G}^{\alpha+H_{+}}Y^{\mathbb{Q}}\right)(s,t)\right]\Big\}
exp⁡{ν22​∫st𝚔H−​(t−u)2​𝑑u−Ysℚ​C​(s,T)−A⁡(s,T)},\displaystyle\exp\left\{\frac{\nu^{2}}{2}\int_{s}^{t}\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(t-u)^{2}\mathrm{d}u-Y^{\mathbb{Q}}_{s}C(s,T)-A(s,T)\right\},

ν​𝚔H−​(T,t)−∂tC⁡(t,T)+C⁡(t,T)​θ+σ22​C2​(t,T)=0,\nu\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(T,t)-\partial_{t}C(t,T)+C(t,T)\theta+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}C^{2}(t,T)=0,

By independence of the driving Brownian motions we have, for any u≤tu\leq t,

𝔼⁡[vt|ℱu]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[v_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{u}] =ξ0​(t)​exp⁡{ν⁡((𝔊−​Zℚ)​(u,t)+(𝒢α+H+​Yℚ)​(u,t))}\displaystyle=\xi_{0}(t)\exp\left\{\nu\left(\left(\mathfrak{G}^{-}Z^{\mathbb{Q}}\right)(u,t)+\left(\mathcal{G}^{\alpha+H_{+}}Y^{\mathbb{Q}}\right)(u,t)\right)\right\}
×𝔼⁡[exp⁡{ν⁡((𝔊−​Zℚ)​(t)−(𝔊−​Zℚ)​(u,t))}]\displaystyle\qquad\times\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\Big\{\nu\left(\left(\mathfrak{G}^{-}Z^{\mathbb{Q}}\right)(t)-\left(\mathfrak{G}^{-}Z^{\mathbb{Q}}\right)(u,t)\right)\Big\}\right]

The last term cancels for A(t,T)=−κθ∫tTC(u,T)dtA(t,T)=-\kappa\theta\int_{t}^{T}C(u,T)\mathrm{d}t, and the Riccati equation ν​𝚔H−​(T,t)−∂tC⁡(t,T)−κ​C​(t,T)+σ22​C2​(t,T)=0\nu\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(T,t)-\partial_{t}C(t,T)-\kappa C(t,T)+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}C^{2}(t,T)=0 remains, with A⁡(T,T)=C⁡(T,T)=0A(T,T)=C(T,T)=0. ∎

Already in the uncorrelated case the computation of 𝔼ℚ​[vt]\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[v_{t}] becomes very costly, having to solve a quadratic ODE (with time-dependent coefficients) for each time tt. In the correlated case there is no hope to obtain any semi-analytic result since one would need to compute cross terms and there is no tool coming from Itô’s calculus available in that case. The approach in this section was essentially top-down, meaning that we specified a form for the market price of volatility risk λ\lambda and deduced the shape of the model with this specification. Unfortunately, our analysis showed that this may ultimately not be so successful as the final form of the model is rather intricate, probably too much so for practical purposes. Alternatively, one may first infer some shape of λ\lambda from market data (short rate of interest, expected returns and instantaneous volatility) and then use it to price options under ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

3. Roughly extracting the Risk Premium from the Market

We now consider the risk premium process λ\lambda deterministic, and obtain a formula linking ℙ\mathbb{P} and ℚ\mathbb{Q} market observable quantities. The following theorem shows how to infer the risk premium from the market using forecasts under ℙ\mathbb{P} and Variance Swap prices under ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

3.1. Estimating the risk premium in rough Bergomi

In this section we work with the rough Bergomi model under ℙ\mathbb{P} and its ℚ\mathbb{Q}-version:

(under ​ℙ){d​StSt=μt​d​t+vt​d​Wtℙ,vt=exp⁡{ν​ZtH},(under ​ℚ){d​StSt=rt​d​t+vt​d​Wtℚ,vt=ξ0​(t)​exp⁡{ν⁡(∫0t𝚔H−​(t−u)​d​Zuℚ+∫0t𝚔H−​(t−u)​λu​du)}.\begin{array}[]{cl}(\text{under }\mathbb{P})&\left\{\begin{array}[]{rl}\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}S_{t}}{S_{t}}&=\displaystyle\mu_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{v_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{P}}_{t},\\ v_{t}&=\displaystyle\exp\left\{\nu Z^{H}_{t}\right\},\\ \end{array}\right.\\ \\ (\text{under }\mathbb{Q})&\left\{\begin{array}[]{rl}\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}S_{t}}{S_{t}}&=\displaystyle r_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{v_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{Q}}_{t},\\ v_{t}&=\displaystyle\xi_{0}(t)\exp\left\{\nu\left(\int_{0}^{t}\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(t-u)\mathrm{d}Z^{\mathbb{Q}}_{u}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathtt{k}_{H_{-}}(t-u)\lambda_{u}\mathrm{d}u\right)\right\}.\end{array}\right.\end{array}

Assuming λ\lambda deterministic, Theorem 3.1 gives an explicit procedure to compute the risk premium. In practice however, we are only able to observe variance swap quotes in discrete times, and hence it is natural to consider λ\lambda piecewise constant.

Assumption 3.2.

Given a time partition {0=T0<T1,…,<Tn=T}\{0=T_{0}<T_{1},...,<T_{n}=T\}, the deterministic process λ\lambda admits the piecewise constant representation

(3.8) λ(t):=∑i=1nλi11{t∈[Ti−1,Ti)},λi∈ℝ for i=1,…,n.\lambda(t):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}1\hskip-5.97508pt{1}_{\{t\in[T_{i-1},T_{i})\}},\quad\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{R}\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n.

Similarly the forward variance admits the piecewise constant representation 𝔼0ℚ[vt]=ξ0(t):=∑i=1nξi11{t∈[Ti−1,Ti)}\mathbb{E}_{0}^{\mathbb{Q}}[v_{t}]=\xi_{0}(t):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}1\hskip-5.97508pt{1}_{\{t\in[T_{i-1},T_{i})\}} with ξi∈ℝ\xi_{i}\in\mathbb{R} for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, where ξi:=𝔙Ti​Ti−𝔙Ti−1​Ti−1Ti−Ti−1\xi_{i}:=\frac{\mathfrak{V}_{T_{i}}T_{i}-\mathfrak{V}_{T_{i-1}}T_{i-1}}{T_{i}-T_{i-1}} and 𝔙T:=𝔼ℚ​[1T​∫0Tvs​𝑑s]\mathfrak{V}_{T}:=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}\left[\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}v_{s}\mathrm{d}s\right] is a market variance swap quote.

We now estimate {λ1,⋯,λn}\{\lambda_{1},\cdots,\lambda_{n}\}. The dataset consists of daily Eurostoxx variance swap quotes for maturities {1M, 3M, 6M, 1Y, 2Y}\{\text{1M, 3M, 6M, 1Y, 2Y}\} (Figures 1 and 2), while Figure 3 shows the daily realised volatility obtained from Oxford-Man institute data.

In order to apply formula (3.1) we need the following ingredients:

(3.9) Parameters ​H,ν,ρ,𝔼ℙ​[vt|ℱ0],𝔼ℚ​[vt|ℱ0].\text{Parameters }H,\nu,\rho,\qquad\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[v_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{0}],\qquad\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[v_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{0}].

So far we have obtained 𝔼ℚ​[vt|ℱ0]\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[v_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{0}] from Variance Swap market quotes. The next step is to estimate (H,ν,ρ)(H,\nu,\rho) using historical time-series. Gatheral, Jaisson and Rosenbaum [14], explain how to estimate H^\widehat{H} and ν^\widehat{\nu} from daily volatility data (Figure 3), and we follow their approach using a 100-day rolling window (Figure 4) and refer the reader to the original paper for details.

To estimate the correlation parameter we use Corr⁡(ZtH−ZsH,∫std​Ws)=ρ​2​HH+\displaystyle\mathrm{Corr}\left(Z^{H}_{t}-Z^{H}_{s},\int_{s}^{t}\mathrm{d}W_{s}\right)=\frac{\rho\sqrt{2H}}{H_{+}}, which allows us to estimate the correlation with the proxy

Figure 6 shows the historical evolution of the risk premium process.

Remark 3.3.

We would like to emphasise that assessing the best method to estimate (3.9) is beyond the scope of this paper. However, as highlighted in the introduction, we stress the importance of Theorem 3.1 towards which this empirical work provides a first step.

Z^tn=Ztℙ−∫0t∧τn(ρ​χu+ρ¯​γu)​𝑑u=Ztℙ−∫0t∧τnλu​𝑑u,\widehat{Z}^{n}_{t}=Z^{\mathbb{P}}_{t}-\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{n}}\Big(\rho\chi_{u}+\overline{\rho}\;\gamma_{u}\Big)\mathrm{d}u=Z^{\mathbb{P}}_{t}-\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{n}}\lambda_{u}\mathrm{d}u,

for t≥0t\geq 0, where Z^n\widehat{Z}^{n} is a ℙ^n\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}-Brownian motion. Furthermore, by Assumption 1.3(ii), we have

(A.2) ℙ^n​(supt∈𝕋Yt≥n)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb{T}}Y_{t}\geq n\right) =ℙ^n​(supt∈𝕋{Y^tn+∫0t∧τnk⁡(t,u)​λu​𝑑u}≥n)\displaystyle=\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb{T}}\left\{\widehat{Y}_{t}^{n}+\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{n}}k(t,u)\lambda_{u}\mathrm{d}u\right\}\geq n\right)
≤ℙ^n​(supt∈𝕋Y^tn+supt∈𝕋{∫0t∧τnk⁡(t,u)​λu​𝑑u}≥n)\displaystyle\leq\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb{T}}\widehat{Y}_{t}^{n}+\sup_{t\in\mathbb{T}}\left\{\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{n}}k(t,u)\lambda_{u}\mathrm{d}u\right\}\geq n\right)
≤ℙ^n​(supt∈𝕋Y^tn≥n−K𝕋),\displaystyle\leq\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb{T}}\widehat{Y}_{t}^{n}\geq n-K_{\mathbb{T}}\right),

Inequality (A.2), in turn, implies ℙ^n​(τn≤T)≤ℙ^n​(τ^n≤T)\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}(\tau_{n}\leq T)\leq\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}(\widehat{\tau}_{n}\leq T), for τ^n:=inf{t≥0,Y^tn=n−K𝕋}\widehat{\tau}_{n}:=\inf\{t\geq 0,\;\widehat{Y}_{t}^{n}=n-K_{\mathbb{T}}\}. Finally, since Z^n\widehat{Z}^{n} is a ℙ^n\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}-Brownian motion, we obtain

limn↑∞ℙ^n​(τn≤T)≤limn↑∞ℙ^n​(τ^n≤T)=limn↑∞ℙ⁡(supt∈𝕋Yt≥n−K𝕋)=0,\lim_{n\uparrow\infty}\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}(\tau_{n}\leq T)\leq\lim_{n\uparrow\infty}\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}(\widehat{\tau}_{n}\leq T)=\lim_{n\uparrow\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb{T}}Y_{t}\geq n-K_{\mathbb{T}}\right)=0,

and it follows that d​ℚd​ℙ\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}} is indeed a true martingale and note that limn↑∞ℙ^n=ℚ\displaystyle\lim_{n\uparrow\infty}\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{n}=\mathbb{Q}. In the sense that the relation (1.8) holds between the ℙ\mathbb{P} and ℚ\mathbb{Q} Brownian motions.
